newsitem.title: MACAU: Macau casino opens despite recent bombing attacks.
newsitem.headline: Macau casino opens despite recent bombing attacks.

text.p: A casino in Portuguese-ruled Macau opened its doors to business on Saturday despite recent bomb and machinegun attacks and an approaching typhoon.
Security was tight at the luxury hotel where the new casino is located. Special police wielding machine-guns were posted at the New Century Hotel in the Taipa district.
"We remain open in spite of the typhoon in order to show that everything is okay here," one of the casino manager told Reuters.
The typhoon, expected to hit the south China coast around midnight (1600 GMT), forced Macau international airport to close and disrupted life in nearby Hong Kong.
Three security guards were injured by machinegun fire outside the hotel on Wednesday when a gunman opened fire from a car.
Three weeks ago, police removed and detonated a bomb planted under a tourist bus outside the same hotel, and the building suffered another bomb scare a week later.
The China-funded hotel was recently taken over by a local consortium which said it planned to open a casino.
Macau police said the attacks were meant as a warning.
In Macau, which earns most of its foreign currency from gambling-related tourism, triads, or secret societies, run protection rackets preying on the casino business.

Recent reports from Macau have said rival triad gangs -- the 14K and the Soi Fong -- are fighting over shares in illegal loansharking and casino rackets, leading to 16 deaths and a spate of fire bombings so far this year.
Home-made bombs were also thrown at Macau's government headquarters and police headquarters this week.
Macau Governor General Vasco Rocha Vieira vowed on Friday his government was determined to combat the bloody triad gang wars that have rocked the tiny enclave.
Rocha Vieira said a new anti-triad law, to take effect on Monday, will give police and courts stronger powers to counter gangland violence and criminal activities.
Macau has been under Portuguese control for four and a half centuries and reverts to Chinese rule in 1999. Neighbouring Hong Kong returned to China on July 1 after 156 years of British colonial rule.
China's chief representative in the enclave, Wang Qiren, said this week that the law and order situation was worrying and that police efforts to tackle the violence were inadequate.
